having tried my best to intuit the motives of the protesters in France today, I am struck by the fact that two of the most  treasured pillars of the European postwar order are colliding: 

1. unfettered immigration, especially from former colonies, justified by historical obligation and postcolonial guilt

2. protecting pensions and the elderly at all costs, even to the point of extreme fiscal strain

now you have first and second generation immigrants, as well as young native french people, taking to the streets because the french state is hell-bent on extracting whatever it can and feeding it into the maw of boomer luxury communism.

the younger generation is being asked to accept a deteriorating deal: pay more, receive less, and abandon the expectation of matching the living standard of their parents or grandparents. 

the young immigrant newcomers have even less incentive to accept any kind this bargain. they are not bought in to the french social contract. they have no common identity with the french boomers they are being asked to sustain. they resent the fact that the entire machinery of the state is designed to exploit the young to serve the old. 

the old do not care about the immigrants enough to trade away any of their entitlements for them. they have the advantage as they wield the franchise reliably and their share of the electorate is only growing, so they won't accept a decline in their own standard of living to fund a future they will never live to see. 

now these two groups are on a collision course. 

ironically, immigration was intended to ameliorate the worsening fiscal picture brought about by a demographic transition. but this did not happen. studies have repeatedly shown that immigrants do increase aggregate GDP (by simple brute force, by adding to population), but not the fiscal picture [1]. the most comprehensive paper using real-world data [2] segments immigrant types to France and finds non-EU immigrants to be persistently fiscally negative. EU immigrants by contrast are the most fiscally positive group, meaning that studies that consider immigrants as a whole are masking the negative impact of non-western immigrants (and Algeria, Morocco, and Tunisia rank #1 and #2 and #4. Africa accounts for 50% of the 8 million immigrants living in France today.) 

immigration has not caused France's fiscal crisis. but it hasn't bettered the economic picture at all – it has deteriorated it somewhat – and it has created a combustible demographic that has little allegiance to the French nation. far from helping France deal with its aging workforce, immigration has added fiscal burden and created a permanent, non-assimilated disenfranchised underclass. the original justifications for immigration – labor scarcity, postcolonial obligation, and more recently workforce aging – have largely failed to manifest the promised results. 

the pro-immigrationist policy has been defended in Brussels as necessary to defend the welfare state, but it has expanded the population making claims on the state, without eliminating the need for fiscal adjustments. 

France now has an aging electorate aiming to preserve the benefits it was promised, mingled with a younger more diverse population that questions whether it will ever receive a similar deal. the young are vastly outmatched at the ballot box and so they take to the streets. 

the french establishment is now trying to preserve a tenuous status quo: unlimited intergenerational obligations alongside a neverending immigration regime that continually changes the composition of the society intended to honor those obligations. the immigration regime also actively worsens the fiscal picture while creating these cultural fractures and inculcating a society more prone to sectarian violence.  

the french state will have to renegotiate its social contract and disempower one of these groups. electoral gravity suggests that the old will continue to win until France finally reaches default and creditors renegotiate the welfare state for them. 

the major contenders in 27 take different approaches to this tradeoff: 
- the right in Le Pen looks to reduce immigration-related expenditure and focus public spending on French citizens, while resisting retirement age increases
- Macron in the center aims to control immigration somewhat and reform pensions by raising retirement age
- Melenchon's left, largely behind the protests this week, denies the tradeoff and aims to keep funding pensions and retirement at 60 while increasing immigration. as France has very little fiscal space it's unclear how this would be paid for

whether the french social contract can be peacefully renegotiated remains to be seen. 

[1] For France, immigrants' net fiscal contribution averaged -0.85% of GDP over 2006-2018 when all public expenditure was allocated (and this includes ALL categories of immigrants including European, American and Asian) See: https://t.co/DZcE2FrRmS

[2] See table 4 (translated below) https://t.co/FccZ1CKiUX

the news will tell you that the left are protesting because "of insufficient school funding" 

This is questionable at best. France has a massive welfare state. Gigantic. They do not lack for public sector expenditure. 

- French public spending accounts for an almost incomprehensible 57.2% of GDP
- the French deficit is 5.1% of GDP and the debt to GDP ratio is 115% 
- France spends more on education on both a relative and absolute basis than the EU average 

France can't meaningfully increase public spending. they are maxed out. Their 10-year bond trades at a higher yield than Italy or Greece, historical basket cases. 

so, it's not about public spending. France is an insanely lavish welfare state to the point of serious dysfunction. 

what's it about then?

If a protocol inside Kraken’s $USDC vault gets exploited, five independent security firms decide whether you get paid back.

With most DeFi vaults, if a protocol underneath gets exploited, you just eat the loss.

The vault runs the strategy and moves your money around for you, but the risk is still yours unless you went out and bought your own cover.

@Firelightfi changes that with a different approach. The vault operator arranges the cover, and everyone in the vault is protected without doing anything extra.

@SentoraHQ already uses it on its USD and RWA vaults, and now it’s live on @krakenfx’s Protected Strategies USDC earn vault, which Sentora curates.

If a covered protocol gets exploited, has an oracle failure, or hits another specified incident, those five firms review what happened.

If they validate the loss, Firelight can pay the vault from its backing capital, which comes from people staking $XRP with Firelight. Their stake gets slashed to cover the payout.

Honestly I think the vault level is the right place for this, because most people were never gonna buy cover on their own anyway.

It doesn’t make the vault risk-free though. Payouts aren’t automatic and cover only applies to specific incidents. There’s also a ceiling, $38M of cover available right now across three strategies.

But if you're comparing DeFi vaults, checking what happens when things go wrong is probably just as important as checking the APY.

tweets.text:
Ben Horowitz: “The most dangerous thing going on in AI is Anthropic and Bill Gates”

“Anybody can go say, ‘AI is going to kill us,’ and you'll be on every major news station and every newspaper and so forth.

I think it's extremely dangerous, though, when it comes from Bill Gates because he is so credible, because he did build Microsoft, and people think of him that way, and then certainly he's been a big political donor, so he has a lot of political juice, particularly on the Democratic side.

The big risk that everybody talks about is that the models are going to recursively self-improve, and then they're going to take off, and then they're going to become so smart and run away from us.

Well, what would be the preconditions for that?

Ali Ghodsi from Databricks had a great formulation of, ‘Well, what would be the preconditions for that?’

And he had four preconditions.

One is that the next model has to require fewer GPUs than the last.

The second thing is the next model has to take less time to train.

And then the accuracy of the next model has to be better than the last, so it's got to be a better model.

And then finally, it's gotta keep happening again and again and again.

Zero of those four have been met.

We're not on track for any of those four to be met, and so we're really talking about a risk that's entirely theoretical at this point that we're not mapping to.”
